2027-07-24.title: Saturday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Sharbel Makhluf
readings: See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you
To the upright I will show the saving power of God
Let both of them grow together until the harvest
2027-07-24.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 16 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Sharbel (Charbel) Makhluf, a Lebanese Maronite monk, priest and hermit, may be kept (white if kept), or the optional Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The Syro-Malankara Church of Kerala also remembers St Sharbel today, in the Panchangam of the Church. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering; Psalm 50 has the same verse numbers in the Lectionary. Tomorrow, the Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year B), the Gospel turns to John 6, the bread of life. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-24.verse: Then he took the book of the covenant, and read it in the hearing of the people; and they said, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” Moses took the blood and dashed it on the people, and said, “See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you in accordance with all these words.”
theo: Today's first reading ends the long scene of the giving of the law at Sinai with the sealing of the covenant, and it is one of the great liturgies of the Old Testament. Moses has received the words and the ordinances of the Lord, and he comes down to tell the people everything. They answer “with one voice”: “All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do.” Moses does not let the words go with the wind: he “wrote down all the words of the Lord.” Early the next morning he builds an altar at the foot of the mountain, and around it he sets up twelve pillars, “corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel.” The altar is God's side of the covenant, the pillars are the people's; between them is the sacrifice. Young men offer burnt offerings and “offerings of well-being,” meals shared in joy with God. Then comes the central action. Moses takes the blood of the sacrifice, which in the Old Testament stands for life, and divides it: half is put in basins; half is dashed against the altar. He reads the “book of the covenant” in the hearing of the people, who answer again, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” In Hebrew, na'aseh ve-nishma: we will do, and we will hear. And then Moses takes the blood in the basins and “dashed it on the people, and said, ‘See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you in accordance with all these words.’” The same blood touches the altar and the people: God and Israel are bound together in one life. The Letter to the Hebrews will remember this moment (Hebrews 9:18–20), and Jesus will use almost the same words at the Last Supper: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24). The Christian Church sees in Sinai a shadow of what Christ does at the Eucharist: the new covenant sealed in his blood, shared at the table. The psalm takes up the same theme from the other side. God summons the earth: “Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice!” and he teaches what pleases him: “Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and pay your vows to the Most High. Call on me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.” The Greek word for thanksgiving is eucharistia. The sacrifice that God most loves is a grateful heart.

In the Gospel Jesus gives another parable of the kingdom, found only in Matthew: the wheat and the weeds. A householder sows good seed in his field; “while everybody was asleep, an enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and then went away.” The weed meant here, probably the bearded darnel, looks very like wheat until the ears appear, when the difference is clear. “So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared as well.” The slaves ask, with amazement, “Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where, then, did these weeds come from?” The householder answers, “An enemy has done this.” Evil in the world and in the Church is not God's doing; there is an enemy. And the slaves, quite naturally, ask, “Then do you want us to go and gather them?” The householder says, “No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest.” Only at harvest will the reapers separate them, and the wheat be gathered “into my barn.” Jesus will explain the parable in a few days (Matthew 13:36–43). Meanwhile the point is plain: patience. The Church on earth is a field where good and bad grow together, and it is not our work to decide, before the time, who is wheat and who is weed. Often we cannot tell: the harsh person may be the one who most needs mercy, and a seeming saint may be a weed. The Catechism teaches that the Church is “at once holy and always in need of being purified” (Catechism 827, quoting Lumen Gentium 8). This is not an excuse for indifference to evil: the householder knows there is an enemy, and the harvest will come. But it is a strong teaching on God's patience, which gives everyone time to repent: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord God, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). Today the Church remembers one who quietly allowed God to cultivate him: St Sharbel Makhluf, a Lebanese Maronite monk and hermit of the nineteenth century, who spent his last twenty-three years in a mountain hermitage, hidden and silent, and who now draws pilgrims of all faiths to his tomb at Annaya.
outline: Ask: when you promise God something at Mass, how much of it do you actually do the next day?
Israel's two answers at Sinai; the people who hear and do.
Point 2 · The blood of the covenant
Moses' altar, the sprinkled blood, and the Eucharist of the new covenant.
The enemy sows weeds; the householder's patience and the harvest.
Point 4 · St Sharbel, hidden in prayer
A Maronite monk who lived in silence and obedience, and the fruit of a hidden life.
live: After the readings of tomorrow's Sunday Mass, choose one thing you will do in the week that follows, and tell one person about it.
Pray today by name for one person who annoys or troubles you, and ask God to give both of you time to grow. Do not give up on the good that is in them.
Spend at least ten minutes in silence today, with no phone, radio or conversation, speaking only to your Father who is in secret.
saints: Born Youssef Antoun Makhlouf on 8 May 1828 in Bekaa Kafra, a mountain village in northern Lebanon, to a poor family; his father died when he was three. As a young man he left home to join the Lebanese Maronite Order, took the name Sharbel (Charbel), a name of an early martyr of Syria, and was ordained priest in 1859. He lived for sixteen years in the monastery of St Maron at Annaya, and from 1875 until his death in a hermitage nearby, in obedience to his superiors, in silence, poverty and prayer, with deep devotion to the Eucharist and to Our Lady. While celebrating the Divine Liturgy on 16 December 1898 he suffered a stroke; he died on 24 December 1898. Soon after his death a light was reported at his tomb, and many healings have been reported there among Christians and Muslims alike. Beatified in 1965 at the close of the Second Vatican Council, and canonised in 1977, both by Pope Paul VI. The Maronite Church is one of the Eastern Catholic Churches in communion with Rome; its liturgy belongs to the ancient Syriac tradition of Antioch, which still uses Syriac, a later form of Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. Optional memorial in the Roman Calendar on 24 July.
2027-07-24.prayer: God of the covenant, you bound yourself to your people at Sinai by the sprinkled blood, and in your Son you sealed a new and everlasting covenant. Make us a people who say, We will do, and then do what we say. Lord Jesus, you teach us patience with the wheat and the weeds; give us the patience of the householder and the mercy of the Father who wills that all should come to repentance. Through the prayers of St Sharbel, who sought you in silence and hidden prayer, teach us to seek you in secret and to give you a sacrifice of thanksgiving. Keep Lebanon and all the Middle East in your peace. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest takes the cup and says the words of Jesus: this is the chalice of my blood, the blood of the new and eternal covenant, which will be poured out for you and for many. Moses sprinkled blood on the people; in the Eucharist Christ gives us his own blood to drink, so that his life flows in us. The Church calls this sacrifice a Eucharist, a thanksgiving, because it is the thanksgiving for all that the Lord has done. St Sharbel, a hermit, never lived without the Eucharist: he said that the Mass was the most important hour of his day, and he is said to have prepared for it, and to have given thanks after it, for long hours.

quick: Moses writes down the words of the Lord, builds an altar with twelve pillars, and reads the book of the covenant; the people say: we will do, and we will be obedient.
Moses sprinkles the blood of the sacrifice on the altar and on the people: the blood of the covenant.

2027-07-24.question: Do I judge quickly who is wheat and who is a weed, or do I leave judgement to God and pray for everyone?
kidsaint: Sharbel was a shepherd boy in the mountains of Lebanon, a country in the Middle East. He loved to pray alone in a cave while his sheep grazed. When he grew up he became a monk, and later a hermit, which means a person who lives alone to pray. He lived in a tiny room on a mountain, ate very simple food and prayed for hours for everyone in the world. When he died, many people came to his tomb to pray, and many were healed. Lesson: a prayer said quietly and secretly is not lost; God sees it and uses it for the good of many.

family.explain: Jesus told a story about a farmer who planted good wheat in his field. In the night, an enemy came and planted weeds in the same field. When the plants grew, the farmer's workers saw the weeds, too. They asked: should we pull them out? The farmer said: no, you will pull up the wheat too. Wait until the harvest. In God's field, good people and bad people are growing side by side, and God is patient with all. He gives everyone time to change.
family.intention: We pray for people who find it hard to be good, and for the patience to wait for them.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone we are quick to judge? What can we do this week to give them a chance?”

illus: A rice farmer from Kuttanad, an old man named Ouseph, used to tell his grandchildren that the worst weed in the paddy field is the grass that looks exactly like the young rice. A new worker, hired in a hurry, once pulled up half the good seedlings in one morning, because they all looked alike to her. Ouseph never scolded her. He said: in the first weeks only the Lord can tell them apart. We must wait until the ear shows. Years later the same woman supervised the field herself, and was known for the patience with which she weeded. When someone in the parish spoke harshly about a neighbour, she would say: wait until the harvest. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: God of the covenant, you pour out your life for us. Lord Jesus, give us the patience of the householder and the thankfulness of those who offer a sacrifice of praise. Amen.
share: All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do (Exodus 24:3). What have I said to God that I have not yet done?
See the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8). What does it mean for me that Christ's blood binds me to God and to my brothers and sisters?
Let both of them grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). Whom do I judge too fast, and how can I give them time?
pm.resp: To the upright I will show the saving power of God.
interc: For the Church, a field where wheat and weeds grow together, that she may be patient and holy.
For the Maronite Church and the Christians of Lebanon, and for peace in Lebanon and in the Middle East, through the intercession of St Sharbel.
For those who live in silence and hidden prayer, hermits, monks and nuns, that their prayer may bear fruit.
For those who are sick, that through the intercession of St Sharbel they may find healing and hope.
For our group, that we may be doers of the word and not hearers only.
pm.close: Father, you made a covenant with your people by sacrifice and sealed it in the blood of your Son. Make us faithful to your word and patient with one another. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, the first reading is the sealing of the covenant at Sinai. Moses tells the people all the words of the Lord, and they answer with one voice: all the words that the Lord has spoken we will do (Exodus 24:3). Moses writes everything down. In the morning he builds an altar, with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, and the sacrifice is offered. Then Moses reads the book of the covenant, and the people say again: we will do, and we will be obedient. How many times have we said at Mass, yes, Lord, we will do it? And how many times have we done it?

Then Moses does something dramatic. He takes the blood of the sacrifice, half on the altar, and half he sprinkles on the people: see the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you (Exodus 24:8). Blood is life. The same life touches the altar, which is God's, and the people. This is what Jesus does at the Last Supper: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:24). At every Mass, the same blood is given to us, not sprinkled on our skin but taken into our lives. The Eucharist makes the covenant new every day, and it asks us to do what we promise.

In the Gospel Jesus tells of an enemy who sowed weeds among the wheat. The workers want to pull them out at once. But the owner says: no, you will uproot the wheat with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest. This is God's patience. In our families, our parishes and even in our own hearts, the wheat and the weeds grow together. We want to uproot the people who annoy us. God waits, because he wants everyone to be saved. And he gives us time too. Whom do I judge too quickly? And who has been patient with me?

Today we remember St Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of Lebanon, a hermit who lived in silence for twenty-three years in a little cell on a mountain. He did not judge the world; he prayed for it, hidden with his Father who is in secret. When he died, God showed that this quiet prayer was not lost: many people were healed at his tomb, Christians and non-Christians alike. Let us pray with Sharbel for Lebanon and for peace, and let us ask for the grace to be doers of the word, patient with each other and faithful in secret prayer. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus told a story about a farmer who planted good wheat. At night an enemy planted weeds. The workers wanted to pull them out right away, but the farmer said: wait, or you will pull up the wheat too! God is like that farmer. He is patient with us and gives us time to grow. Today we also remember St Sharbel, a monk who loved to pray alone in a little room on a mountain. He prayed for everybody, and God heard his prayer. Let us also set aside a few quiet minutes today to talk to God.

intro: Theme: “See the blood of the covenant.”
We will do, the blood of the covenant, the patient householder, and the hidden prayer of a hermit.

q: Moses came and told the people all the words of the Lord and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, “All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do.”
But be doers of the word, and not merely hearers who deceive themselves.

He said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
points.apply: At Communion this Sunday, say silently: Lord, I belong to your covenant, and I will do what you say.

q: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord God, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?
The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some think of slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance.
points.apply: Pray by name this week for someone you have judged harshly, asking God to give them time and you patience.

sub: Your Father who is in secret.
q: Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and pay your vows to the Most High. Call on me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.
But whenever you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
points.apply: Take ten minutes of silence each day this week and pray for Lebanon and for peace.

concl: God seals a covenant with his people in blood at Sinai, and in Christ he seals the new covenant in the Eucharist: we say we will do, and we are called to do it.
The Lord is patient with the wheat and the weeds; St Sharbel shows how a life hidden in prayer bears fruit for many.
2027-07-24.resolve: Each day this week do one thing you have heard from the word, be patient with someone, and keep ten minutes of silence.
